title: Building a Competitive Financial Centre: Strategy, Regulation and Investment Promotion
summary: An eight-module programme helping ministries and investment promotion agencies build a competitive, reputable financial centre and measure the results.
intro: This training programme equips ministries and investment promotion agencies to build a competitive, reputable financial centre: setting strategy, protecting regulatory standards, attracting fund managers and fintechs, and measuring what success looks like.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give officials responsible for financial centre development a practical framework for positioning a jurisdiction, attracting financial business and building the legal, tax, talent and regulatory foundations that sustain it. Participants leave able to design a credible strategy, understand how international firms choose where to locate, avoid the reputational traps of competing on lax standards, and measure the results.
sections.What It Covers: What makes a financial centre competitive, strategic positioning and niche selection, regulatory reputation and the role of the regulator, licensing speed versus standards, legal, tax and market infrastructure, talent and immigration, attracting fund managers, fintechs and digital asset firms, international standards and blacklists, and measuring success.
Intended Audience: Staff of investment promotion agencies, financial centre development bodies and economic development boards
Officials in finance and economy ministries responsible for financial sector growth strategy
Senior officials and advisers who oversee financial centre strategy and its relationship with the regulator
Learning Objectives: Explain the factors that determine where financial firms choose to locate
Assess a jurisdiction's competitive strengths, weaknesses and credible niches
Evaluate the trade-offs between licensing speed, regulatory standards and reputation
Identify the legal, tax, talent and infrastructure foundations a financial centre needs
Design an investment promotion approach for fund managers, fintechs and other target sectors
Define success measures and an action plan for financial centre strategy
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as an intensive programme over two to three days or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a briefing with comparative case studies and practical exercises, ending in a strategy workshop, and modules can be selected or tailored to the jurisdiction's target sectors.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of economic development, investment promotion or financial services policy is helpful. No technical background in regulation is required.
Core Reading: IOSCO (2017), Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation
FATF (2012, updated), International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation: The FATF Recommendations
OECD (2021), Statement on a Two-Pillar Solution to Address the Tax Challenges Arising from the Digitalisation of the Economy
OECD (2023), OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct

modules.title: What Makes a Financial Centre Competitive
modules.summary: The economics of financial centres, how international firms take location decisions, and the factors that distinguish global, regional and specialist centres.
objectives: Explain the agglomeration economics behind financial centres
Describe how firms decide where to locate people, entities and activities
Distinguish global, regional, offshore and niche financial centres
syllabus: Agglomeration, clusters and network effects
Location decisions: market access, talent, cost, regulation and tax
Financial centre indices: what they measure and what they miss
Case studies of centres that grew, specialised or declined

modules.title: Strategy and Positioning
modules.summary: How to develop a financial centre strategy grounded in evidence, choose credible niches and align ministries, agencies, the regulator and industry behind it.
objectives: Diagnose the jurisdiction's current position using data and stakeholder evidence
Select target sectors and niches that build on genuine strengths
Design governance for the strategy across government, regulator and industry
syllabus: Diagnostic tools: sector mapping, benchmarking and competitor analysis
Niche selection: funds, insurance, fintech, digital assets and sustainable finance
Public-private partnership models and industry bodies
Avoiding over-reliance on a single sector or source of business

modules.title: Regulatory Reputation and the Role of the Regulator
modules.summary: Why regulatory quality and independence are a competitive asset, how reputation is built and lost, and how government should frame the regulator's role in growth without compromising its independence.
objectives: Explain why international firms and investors value a credible regulator
Assess the risks of competitiveness or growth objectives for regulators
Define a constructive relationship between promotion bodies and the regulator
syllabus: Regulatory reputation as the foundation of market access
Growth and competitiveness objectives: design and safeguards
Separation of promotion and supervision functions
Case studies of reputational damage from regulatory failure

modules.title: Licensing Speed, Standards and the Race to the Bottom
modules.summary: How to make authorisation efficient and predictable without lowering standards, and why competing on light-touch licensing attracts the wrong firms and invites international scrutiny.
objectives: Identify what makes authorisation slow and what genuinely speeds it up
Evaluate service standards, pre-application engagement and fast-track routes
Assess the risks of attracting firms that seek weak oversight
syllabus: Authorisation service standards and transparency
Pre-application support, innovation hubs and sandboxes
Substance requirements and avoiding letterbox entities
Signals of a race to the bottom and how standard-setters respond

modules.title: Legal, Tax and Market Infrastructure
modules.summary: The legal, judicial, tax and market infrastructure that international firms expect, from flexible corporate and fund vehicles to treaty networks, courts and trading and settlement systems.
objectives: Identify the legal vehicles and judicial arrangements firms look for
Explain tax neutrality, treaty networks and international tax standards
Assess the market infrastructure and connectivity a centre requires
syllabus: Company, partnership, trust and fund vehicle legislation
Commercial courts, arbitration and insolvency regimes
Tax neutrality, treaties, global minimum tax and transparency standards
Exchanges, settlement, custody and digital infrastructure

modules.title: Talent, Skills and Quality of Life
modules.summary: How access to skilled people determines a centre's growth, and the immigration, education, professional development and quality-of-life policies that attract and retain talent.
objectives: Assess the talent needs of target sectors and current gaps
Evaluate immigration, visa and professional recognition policies
Design skills pipelines with universities, industry and professional bodies
syllabus: Talent mapping for funds, fintech, compliance and technology roles
Work permits, fast-track visas and recognition of qualifications
Education, apprenticeships and professional certification
Cost of living, connectivity and quality of life as location factors

modules.title: Attracting Fund Managers, Fintechs and Digital Asset Firms
modules.summary: Practical investment promotion for priority sectors: understanding each sector's decision-making, tailoring the proposition, and conducting due diligence on the firms being attracted.
objectives: Explain what fund managers, fintechs and digital asset firms look for
Design a targeted value proposition and promotion campaign
Apply integrity and reputational due diligence to prospective firms
syllabus: Fund domiciliation, management and servicing decisions
Fintech and digital asset firm location drivers
Promotion tools: missions, events, landing support and incentives
Integrity checks on promoters, beneficial owners and business models

modules.title: International Standards, Reputation and Measuring Success
modules.summary: Brings the programme together by examining how international lists, assessments and peer reviews affect a centre's reputation, how success should be measured, and what a credible action plan contains.
objectives: Assess the impact of FATF, tax transparency and financial sector assessments on reputation
Define meaningful success measures beyond licence numbers
Produce a financial centre strategy action plan
syllabus: FATF lists, tax non-cooperative lists and their commercial consequences
Indicators: jobs, tax, exports, substance and assets under management
Monitoring, evaluation and reporting to ministers
Workshop: a financial centre strategy and action plan
